In [[mathematics]], in the realm of [[group theory]], a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] is said to be '''capable''' if it is isomorphic to the quotient {{Math|''G'' / Z(''G'')}} of some group {{Mvar|''G''}} by its [[Center (group theory)|center]]. 

These groups were first studied by [[Reinhold Baer]], who showed that a [[finite group|finite]] [[abelian group]] is capable if and only if it is a [[direct product of groups|product]] of [[cyclic group]]s of [[order of a group|orders]] ''n''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''n''<sub>''k''</sub> where ''n''<sub>''i''</sub> [[divisor|divides]] ''n''<sub>''i''{{hairsp}}+1</sub> and ''n''<sub>''k''{{hairsp}}−1</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''n''<sub>''k''</sub>.

An equivalent condition for a group to be capable is if it occurs as the [[inner automorphism]] group of some group. To see this, note that the canonical surjective map <math>G \to \operatorname{Inn}(G)</math> has kernel {{Math|Z(''G'')}}; by the [[First Isomorphism Theorem|first isomorphism theorem]], {{Math|''G'' / Z(''G'')}} is equivalent to <math>\operatorname{Inn}(G)</math>.
